title: Case: Building a “dream team” – employee resourcing at Netflix
text: Adapted from Wilton (2018). Netflix's culture centres on independent decision-making by employees, sharing information openly and broadly, selecting people who are very candid with each other, keeping only highly effective people and avoiding rules. HR aims to build a “dream team” in which every colleague is outstanding at the job and collaborates well – the place where people learn and perform best.

Besides “best practice” hiring and collaboration, Netflix is known for the “keeper test”. Instead of ratings or rankings, managers answer one question: if this team member were about to leave for another firm, would I fight hard to keep them? Employees who do not pass – those performing merely adequately – are promptly given a generous severance package so the position can be filled by someone better. The logic is that of a sports team, not a family: every player must be excellent in their position.

A possible concern is that employees become risk-averse for fear of mistakes. Netflix argues the opposite: performance is judged on the expected overall contribution, people with a strong track record get leeway during a temporary dip, and employees are asked to stay through short-term dips of the company.

Under the heading “Inclusion”, Netflix expects employees to collaborate with people of diverse backgrounds, use differing perspectives for better decisions, focus on talent and values rather than similarity to themselves, be curious about how backgrounds affect work, recognise and work past their own biases, and step in when someone is marginalised.

The reward strategy pays employees at the top of their personal market: what Netflix estimates to be the highest pay they could earn at peer firms. Pay is recalibrated every year based on individual performance and the labour market.
